title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Overview: Three Papers, One Story
This lecture covers three closely connected papers that develop and debate a radical proposal about visual crowding:








Paper
Key contribution




Cicchini, Chopin, & Burr (2022)
Crowding = optimal Bayesian integration (orientation)


Cicchini, D’Errico, & Burr (2024)
Same framework extended to color


Ozkirli et al. (2025) + Cicchini reply
Replication debate → “flexible integrator”





The thread: Is crowding a processing bottleneck that destroys information, or an optimal integration strategy that can actually improve perception?

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Traditional View of Crowding
Crowding = inability to identify peripheral targets when flanked by nearby items.

The dominant view: crowding is a bottleneck — information is compulsory pooled and lost
Nearby items are mixed together indiscriminately
Crowding should always hurt perception


Problems with this view:

Some studies show perception improves under crowding (Manassi et al., 2012; Greenwood et al., 2017)
Blind pooling should add noise — but identical flankers sometimes reduce it
The bottleneck model cannot explain why effects depend on target–flanker similarity

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
The Radical Proposal
Cicchini et al.’s claim: Crowding is optimal Bayesian integration.
The visual system computes a weighted average of target and flanker information:

Weights depend on reliability of each source
Weights depend on similarity between items
When flankers match the target → integration reduces noise


This is the same logic as cue combination in multisensory integration — but applied to spatial neighbors in crowding.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Three Testable Predictions
If crowding = Bayesian integration:








Prediction
Pattern
Why?




Bias
Derivative-of-Gaussian (DoG)
Weight × difference → peaks at intermediate d


Scatter
U-shape (minimum at d = 0)
Identical flankers = extra measurements → less noise


RMSE
Minimum at d = 0
Scatter reduction outweighs bias at d = 0




The scatter prediction is the most radical: it says crowding can make you more precise than seeing the target alone.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Experiment 1 Design





Stimuli: Oriented ovals at 26° eccentricity
Layout: Target + 2 flankers (radial, 5.5° spacing)
Task: Reproduce target orientation (35° or 55°)

Two key manipulations:

\(d\) (flanker-target difference): 19 levels from \(-45°\) to \(+45°\)
\(\sigma\) (reliability via aspect ratio): Rounded (high \(\sigma \approx 13.2°\)) vs Elongated (low \(\sigma \approx 10.0°\))

N = 10 observers, 10,699 trials

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text: Stimulus Configurations

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
What is an Ideal Observer?
An ideal observer is a hypothetical system that performs optimally given the available sensory information.

Knows the forward model perfectly
Knows the prior perfectly
Uses optimal Bayesian inference without error
Has no additional limitations (no neural noise, memory, attention)


Why use it? It sets an upper bound on performance.



Comparison
Interpretation




Human = Ideal
Limited only by early encoding


Human < Ideal
Additional factors limit performance


Human \(\approx\) Ideal
System may be near-optimal

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Response Equation (Eq 2–3)
The ideal response is a weighted combination of target and flankers:
\[R = w \cdot F_1 + w \cdot F_2 + (1 - 2w) \cdot T\]

\(T\) = noisy target representation (\(T + \epsilon_T\), where \(\epsilon_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_T^2)\))
\(F_1, F_2\) = noisy flanker representations (\(F_i + \epsilon_{F_i}\), where \(\epsilon_{F_i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_F^2)\))
\(w\) = integration weight per flanker

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Optimal Weight (Eq 10)
\[w_{opt} = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{2\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_F^2 + 2d^2}\]
Intuition:

Noisier target (\(\sigma_T\) large) → more weight on flankers
Flankers more different (\(d\) large) → less weight on flankers
Noisier flankers (\(\sigma_F\) large) → less weight on flankers

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Predicted Bias: Derivative-of-Gaussian (Eq 7)
Bias = systematic shift toward flankers:
\[\text{Bias}(d) = 2w \cdot d\]

At \(d = 0\): \(w\) maximal, but \(2w \cdot 0 = 0\) → no bias
At small \(d\): \(w\) still large, \(d\) growing → bias increases
At large \(d\): \(w \to 0\) faster than \(d\) grows → bias decreases


This product of a rising (\(d\)) and falling (\(w\)) term produces a Derivative-of-Gaussian (DoG) shape.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Predicted Scatter: U-Shape (Eq 8)
\[S^2 = 2w^2\sigma_F^2 + (1 - 2w)^2\sigma_T^2\]

At \(d = 0\): \(w\) maximal → target noise down-weighted, flanker info supplements → scatter minimized
At large \(d\): \(w \to 0\) → scatter = \(\sigma_T\) (no benefit from flankers)


This produces a U-shape: precision is best when flankers match the target.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
section: Model Simulation: Bias, Scatter, and RMSE
text:
Model Simulation: Bias, Scatter, and RMSE
RMSE combines bias and scatter: \(\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{Bias}^2 + S^2}\)

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Causal Inference Extension (Eq 12–14)
The basic IO always integrates. The Causal Inference (CI) model adds a gating step:
\[w = w_{max} \cdot P(\text{common cause} \mid d)\]
\[P(\text{common cause} \mid d) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{d^2}{2(\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_F^2)}\right)\]

When \(d = 0\): \(P \approx 1\) → integrate fully
When \(d\) is large: \(P \approx 0\) → do not integrate

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
IO vs CI Model Comparison

Key: Basic IO always integrates (\(w > 0\)). CI model gates integration on/off via P(common cause).

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result 1: Assimilative Bias





Bias follows a DoG — zero at \(d = 0\), peaks at ~15–20°
Unreliable target (blue) shows ~3x larger bias
IO fits with 1 free parameter (R² = .93 blue, .37 orange)
CI slightly better with 2 parameters (R² = .97, .73)

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result 2: Precision Improves





Scatter shows a U-shape — minimum at \(d = 0\)
At \(d = 0\): scatter drops below the unflanked baseline
This is the opposite of bottleneck models
IO scatter R² = .71 (blue), .74 (orange)

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result 3: Total Error (RMSE)





Blue (unreliable target) at \(d = 0°\) reaches closer to origin than most orange points
Integration of identical flankers makes an unreliable target perform better than a reliable one alone
“Crowding superiority effect”: identical flankers improve total accuracy beyond the unflanked baseline

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Experiment 2: Distance Effect





4 target-flanker spacings at 26° eccentricity
Dark navy (closest): strongest DoG, same as Exp 1
Cyan (farthest): essentially flat — no integration
Integration only operates within the crowding zone

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Weight Follows Bouma’s Law





Unreliable target (blue): weight ~0.5 close, drops to 0 at far distances
Reliable target (orange): near zero at all distances
Weight crosses zero between 0.3–0.4 → matches Bouma’s critical spacing
Confirms this is crowding, not some other effect

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Experiment 3: Global Integration Design





Question: Do flankers bias the target independently, or does the system compute a flanker average first?

Independent (top): each flanker acts on target separately
Global (bottom): flankers pooled first, then bias target

Key prediction: DoG centered at 0° (independent) vs -15° (global)

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Experiment 3: Global Integration Results





DoG center at -10.8°, close to -15° global prediction
Far from 0° independent prediction
Bootstrap: only 16/1000 iterations closer to 0° → BF = 61.5 for global model
The visual system pools both flankers first, then biases the target

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Experiment 3: Scatter Confirmation





Scatter U-shape center at -14.3°, again near -15°
Consistent with global integration architecture
IO R² = .76 (scatter), CI R² = .78

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Why Test Color?









Cicchini 2022
Cicchini 2024




Feature
Orientation
Color (hue)


Reliability
Shape-based (rounded vs elongated)
Purity-based (desaturated vs saturated)


Task
Reproduce orientation
2AFC: “pinker or greener?”


New evidence
—
Reaction times confirm sensory-level effect




Goal: Show that optimal integration in crowding is not feature-specific — it’s a general strategy.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Experiment Design





Cowhide-textured patches at 17.6° eccentricity
Target + 2 radial flankers, within Bouma’s zone
2AFC: “pinker or greener than reference?”
Flanker-target hue difference: 0°, ±36°, ±72°
Reliability: low purity target (0.12, unreliable) vs high purity (0.34, reliable)
N = 9 + 13, 20,666 trials

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result: Assimilative Bias





Perceived color shifts toward flanker hue
Low purity: slope = 0.76 (flankers dominate)
High purity: slope = 0.53 (target contributes more)
Unreliable targets give more weight to flankers — reliability-weighted integration

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result: Precision Improves (JND)





When flankers match target (\(\delta = 0\)): precision significantly improves
JND drops to 0.45x (low purity) and 0.58x (high purity) of baseline
0.58 \(\approx\) 1/\(\sqrt{3}\) — theoretical optimum for averaging 3 equally reliable items

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result: Total Error





RMSE lowest at \(\delta = 0\): only 0.52x unflanked
For low purity, all flanker conditions have lower RMSE than gray-flanker control
Error rate lowest with matching, soaring with mismatched flankers

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result: RT Confirms Sensory Integration





RT peaks and PSE shifts tightly correlated: r = 0.83–0.84
This rules out a response strategy
Flankers change what the target looks like, not just which button is pressed
New evidence not in 2022

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Against Alternatives
Substitution: Maybe observers accidentally report the flanker? But substitution = mixing two distributions → curve gets broader. Data shows curves getting narrower → system is averaging, not randomly picking.

Greenwood & Parsons (2020): Found crowding hurts precision. But they fixed flanker hue to reference → uncontrolled flanker-target difference across trials. Key: flankers only help when yoked to the target.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Section 3 Summary
All three predictions confirmed for color:







Metric
Result




Bias slope
0.76 (unreliable) vs 0.53 (reliable) — reliability-weighted


JND at \(\delta = 0\)
0.58x baseline \(\approx 1/\sqrt{3}\) (optimal 3-item average)


RMSE at \(\delta = 0\)
0.52x baseline


RT correlation
r = 0.83–0.84 — sensory-level integration




Crowding as optimal integration is not feature-specific — it’s a general spatial strategy.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Ozkirli: Replication Design

Same paradigm: oriented ovals at 26° eccentricity, orientation reproduction
N = 20 naive participants (doubled from N = 10)
All conditions in one session — flanked and unflanked counterbalanced
Same target orientations (35°/55°) for all conditions (fixing a confound)
Per-participant analysis (not aggregated)
13,440 trials total

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Result: M-shape Not U-shape




Top: Cicchini’s original — U-shape, minimum at d = 0.
Bottom: Ozkirli’s replication — M-shape. Scatter similar at d = 0 and 90°, worst at intermediate d.
Bayes factors:

d = ±5–45°: BF = 6450 — decisive deterioration
d = 0°: BF = 0.25 — evidence for no difference
d = 90°: BF = 0.24–0.56 — no difference

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Methodological Criticisms
Cicchini 2022 problems identified by Ozkirli:

Different participant groups for main experiment vs control (separate sessions, 3 years apart)
Different target orientations — flanked used 35°/55°, unflanked used 0°/22.5°/67.5°/90°
Aggregated data — bias and scatter from pooled group data, not per participant


Theoretical concerns:

No superiority effects in prior crowding literature
M-shape consistent with Livne & Sagi (2011), Solomon et al. (2004), Glen & Dakin (2013)

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Cicchini Reply: Replication 1 — Orientation Reproduction




Fig 1a: Each point = one participant. Below diagonal = flankers helped.
Navy circles (N = 7): Same task, identical flankers only, same orientations across conditions.

6/7 below the line
Scatter: 8.0° → 6.2°, 22% reduction
t(6) = 2.8, p = .029, d = 1.16

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Cicchini Reply: Replication 2 — Full Range (2AFC)




Fig 1d: Blue = JND, brown = RMSE. Yellow zone = better than unflanked.

At d = 0°: JND in yellow zone — superiority confirmed
JND ratio 95% CI = [0.64, 0.94], t(8) = 3.15, p = .013
At d = ±30° to ±60°: JND rises above baseline — M-shape confirmed too
Both findings replicate: superiority at d = 0 AND M-shape at dissimilar d

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Cicchini Reply: Replication 3 — Color (2AFC)





2AFC: “pinker or greener than standard?”
At \(\delta = 0\) and ±36°: precision below both unflanked and gray-flanker baselines
Gray flankers provide no benefit — integration requires informative flankers
Extends to color: superiority effect is not orientation-specific

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
The Concession: “Flexible Integrator”
Cicchini et al. acknowledge key limitations:

M-shape confirmed in their own data — “incompatible with a strict Bayesian approach”
Human performance only ~50% of ideal observer predictions
Revised framework: not a rigid ideal observer, but a “flexible integrator”


Against substitution (Ozkirli’s alternative):

If substitution, flanker influence should be same regardless of target reliability
But all datasets show less influence when target is reliable → reliability-weighted
When target = flanker, substitution changes nothing — yet precision still improves

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Common Ground
What both sides agree on:

Identical flankers improve (or at least don’t hurt) precision
M-shape at dissimilar flankers
No irretrievable information loss — crowding is not a simple bottleneck
Global statistics matter — ensemble coding plays a role

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Remaining Disagreements








Issue
Ozkirli
Cicchini




Magnitude at d = 0
No improvement beyond baseline
22% improvement (significant)


Mechanism
Probabilistic substitution
Reliability-weighted integration


Framework
“Crowding only deteriorates”
“Flexible integrator, broadly Bayesian”

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Section 4 Summary







Finding
Status




DoG bias
Replicated by both labs


U-shape scatter
Not replicated — M-shape instead


Superiority at d = 0
Cicchini replicates (3x), Ozkirli finds no change


M-shape at dissimilar d
Both labs agree


Strict IO model
Rejected — replaced by “flexible integrator”

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Key Takeaways
1. Crowding is not a simple bottleneck — it involves reliability-weighted integration of nearby items.

2. Three predictions confirmed across orientation and color: DoG bias, precision improvement, RMSE reduction with identical flankers.


3. The 2025 debate refined the model: not a rigid ideal observer, but a “flexible integrator” that follows Bayesian principles at d = 0 but deviates at large differences.


4. For identical items (d = 0), all parties agree: integration is beneficial or at minimum harmless.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
The Story Arc
\[\text{Optimal (2022)} \longrightarrow \text{Challenged (2025)} \longrightarrow \text{Flexible integrator}\]

2022: Bold claim — crowding is optimal Bayesian integration
2024: Extended to color — not feature-specific
2025 challenge: M-shape, not U-shape; no superiority in replication
2025 reply: Superiority at d = 0 replicated 3x; M-shape conceded at large d
Current status: “Flexible integrator” — broadly Bayesian, clearly beneficial for identical items

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Visual crowding — the inability to identify peripheral targets surrounded by nearby items — is traditionally viewed as a processing bottleneck. Cicchini, Chopin, & Burr (2022, Nature Communications) proposed a radical alternative: crowding is optimal Bayesian integration.






ImportantThe Core Claim



The visual system doesn’t blindly mix nearby items. It computes a weighted average of target and flanker information, where the weight depends on:

Reliability of each source (noisy target → lean more on flankers)
Similarity between items (different flankers → ignore them)

When flankers match the target, this averaging reduces noise — crowding actually helps.


The paper presents two models and two fitting functions:








Component
Equations
What it does




Ideal Observer (IO)
Eq 1–11
Always integrates, weight decreases smoothly with difference


Causal Inference (CI)
Eq 12–17
Adds a gate: integrate only if items likely share a common cause


Fitting functions
Eq 18–19
DoG for bias, Gaussian for scatter — used to fit empirical data









TipWhat We’ll Build



By the end of this demo, you’ll have working R functions for every equation in the paper, and you’ll see how they produce the three key predictions: DoG bias, U-shaped scatter, and RMSE minimum at d = 0.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
The Model Setup
Consider a display with three items arranged radially in the periphery:

Target (T): The item the observer must report (e.g., its orientation)
Flanker 1 (F₁) and Flanker 2 (F₂): Neighboring items that may influence the report

Each item’s representation is noisy:

Target: perceived as \(T + \epsilon_T\), where \(\epsilon_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_T^2)\)
Flankers: perceived as \(F_i + \epsilon_{F_i}\), where \(\epsilon_{F_i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_F^2)\)







NoteWhat do σ_T and σ_F represent?



In the experiment, rounded ovals are hard to judge (\(\sigma \approx 13.2°\)) and elongated ovals are easy (\(\sigma \approx 10.0°\)). These are measured empirically from single-target trials, not assumed.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 1: RMSE Decomposition
Total RMS error (\(E\)) can be decomposed into bias (\(B\)) and precision (scatter standard deviation: \(S\)), whose squares sum to give total squared error:
\[E = \sqrt{B^2 + S^2} \tag{1}\]






ImportantKey Equation



This decomposition is the foundation of the paper’s analysis. Crowding affects bias and scatter differently — you can’t see the full picture by measuring only one.


Concrete example: If bias = 3° and scatter = 4°, then RMSE = \(\sqrt{9 + 16}\) = 5°.



Bias (B)
Scatter (S)
RMSE (E)

4°
5.0°

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 2: General Weighted Response
The ideal response (\(R\)) is a weighted combination of target and flankers:
\[R = w_1 F_1 + w_2 F_2 + (1 - w_1 - w_2) T \tag{2}\]
The weights sum to 1, ensuring the response is a proper weighted average.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 3: Equal-Weight Simplification
Since the two flankers had the same aspect ratio, they should be weighted equally (\(w_1 = w_2 = w\)):
\[R = w F_1 + w F_2 + (1 - 2w) T \tag{3}\]






NoteWhy equal weights?



Both flankers are at the same distance from the target and have the same shape (same σ). There’s no reason to treat one differently from the other.


Parameter table:



Symbol
Meaning
Range




\(w\)
Weight per flanker
0 to ~0.33


\(1 - 2w\)
Weight on target
~0.33 to 1


\(T\)
Target orientation
Degrees


\(F_1, F_2\)
Flanker orientations
Degrees

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equations 4–7: Deriving the Bias
Equation 4 — Mean response:
\[\mu_R = w(\mu_1 + \mu_2) + (1 - 2w)\mu_T \tag{4}\]
Equation 5 — Bias = mean response minus true target:
\[B = \mu_R - x_T = w(\mu_1 + \mu_2 - 2\mu_T) \tag{5}\]
Equation 6 — Define \(d\) as the average flanker–target difference:
\[d = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} - \mu_T \tag{6}\]
Equation 7 — Bias in terms of \(d\):
\[B = 2wd \tag{7}\]






NoteWhy is bias = 2wd?



Each flanker pulls the response by \(w \cdot d\) (weight times difference). Two flankers → \(2wd\). More weight → more pull. Larger difference → more pull. But since \(w\) decreases with \(d\) (Eq 10), the product \(2wd\) traces a derivative-of-Gaussian shape.


Concrete example: If \(w = 0.25\) and \(d = 10°\), then bias = \(2 \times 0.25 \times 10 = 5°\). The response is pulled 5° toward the flankers.


Code
compute_bias <- function(w, d) {
  2 * w * d
}

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 8: Scatter
Since \(R\) is a weighted sum of independent random variables, its variance follows \(\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y)\):
\[S^2 = 2w^2 \sigma_F^2 + (1 - 2w)^2 \sigma_T^2 \tag{8}\]






NoteWhy are the coefficients squared?



Variance measures squared deviations. When you multiply a random variable by a constant \(a\), the variance is multiplied by \(a^2\), not \(a\). This is why \(w\) becomes \(w^2\) and \((1-2w)\) becomes \((1-2w)^2\).


Concrete example: If \(w = 0.25\), \(\sigma_T = 13°\), \(\sigma_F = 10°\):

Flanker contribution: \(2 \times 0.25^2 \times 100 = 12.5\)
Target contribution: \((1 - 0.5)^2 \times 169 = 42.25\)
Total: \(S = \sqrt{12.5 + 42.25} = \sqrt{54.75} = 7.4°\)

Compare to no flankers (\(w = 0\)): \(S = \sigma_T = 13°\). The flankers reduced scatter from 13° to 7.4°!


Code
compute_scatter <- function(w, sigma_T, sigma_F) {
  sqrt(2 * w^2 * sigma_F^2 + (1 - 2 * w)^2 * sigma_T^2)
}

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equations 9–10: Optimal Weight
Equation 9 — RMSE² expanded:
\[E^2 = 4w^2 d^2 + 2w^2 \sigma_F^2 + (1 - 2w)^2 \sigma_T^2 \tag{9}\]


Code
total_error_sq <- function(w, d, sigma_T, sigma_F) {
  4 * w^2 * d^2 + 2 * w^2 * sigma_F^2 + (1 - 4*w + 4*w^2) * sigma_T^2
}


Equation 10 — Minimizing \(E^2\) by setting \(dE^2/dw = 0\):
\[w_{opt} = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{2\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_F^2 + 2d^2} \tag{10}\]






ImportantKey Equation: Optimal Weight



This is the heart of the model. The weight balances three factors:








Factor
Effect on \(w\)
Intuition




Large \(\sigma_T\) (unreliable target)
\(w\) increases
Lean more on flankers


Large \(\sigma_F\) (unreliable flankers)
\(w\) decreases
Flankers aren’t helpful


Large \(d\) (different flankers)
\(w\) decreases
Flankers carry irrelevant info





Concrete examples:


Code
optimal_weight <- function(sigma_T, sigma_F, d) {
  sigma_T^2 / (2 * sigma_T^2 + sigma_F^2 + 2 * d^2)
}




Code

  13.2,     10.0,     0,
  13.2,     10.0,     15,
  13.2,     10.0,     45,
  10.0,     13.2,     0,
  10.0,     10.0,     0
)

  mutate(

      sigma_T == 13.2 & d == 0  ~ "Unreliable T, identical flankers",

      sigma_T == 13.2 & d == 45 ~ "Unreliable T, very different",
      sigma_T == 10.0 & sigma_F == 13.2 ~ "Reliable T, unreliable F",
      sigma_T == 10.0 & sigma_F == 10.0 ~ "Equal reliability"
    )

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 11: Regression to the Mean
The paper also found regression to the mean (responses pulled toward 45°). The full response equation adds a regression factor \(\rho\) and a sub-optimality scaling \(\alpha\):
\[R = \alpha \rho (w F_1 + w F_2 + (1 - 2w) T) + (1 - \rho) \cdot 45 \tag{11}\]






WarningWhen to use Eq 11 vs Eq 3



Eq 11 is for fitting real data (with regression to the mean and sub-optimal behaviour). In our simulations below, we use the pure model (Eq 3 + 10) to show the core predictions without these corrections.

Simulation 1: Bias (Derivative-of-Gaussian)
The bias should follow a DoG pattern: zero at \(d = 0\), peaking at intermediate \(d\), returning toward zero at large \(d\).


Code

sigma_F <- 10
d_range <- seq(-90, 90, by = 1)

sim1 <- tibble(

ggplot(sim1, aes(x = d, y = bias)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "#DC143C") +

The S-shaped curve shows assimilative bias. At intermediate differences (~20–30°), responses are maximally pulled toward the flankers. At very large differences, the flankers are too dissimilar to integrate, so bias drops back toward zero.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 12: Maximum Likelihood Weight
When two sources are known to come from the same cause, the optimal weight for source \(A\) is:
\[w^{max}_A = \frac{\sigma_B^2}{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2} \tag{12}\]






NoteHow does this differ from Eq 10?



Eq 10 weights one flanker among three items (target + 2 flankers) and includes a \(d^2\) term. Eq 12 is the classic two-source MLE weight — no \(d^2\) because the common cause assumption guarantees \(d = 0\).




Code
mle_weight <- function(sigma_A, sigma_B) {
  sigma_B^2 / (sigma_A^2 + sigma_B^2)
}


Concrete example: If \(\sigma_T = 13°\) and \(\sigma_F = 10°\), then \(w_{max} = 100 / (169 + 100) = 0.372\). The more reliable flanker gets 37% weight.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equations 13–14: Common Cause Probability
Equation 13 — Full Bayesian with prior \(P(S) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_P, \sigma_P^2)\):
\[P(A, B \mid C = 1) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{(\mu_A - \mu_B)^2 \sigma_P^2 + (\mu_A - \mu_P)^2 \sigma_B^2 + (\mu_B - \mu_P)^2 \sigma_A^2}{\sigma_A^2 \sigma_B^2 + \sigma_A^2 \sigma_P^2 + \sigma_B^2 \sigma_P^2}\right) \tag{13}\]
The three numerator terms penalize different mismatches:



Term
Meaning




\((\mu_A - \mu_B)^2 \sigma_P^2\)
A and B differ from each other


\((\mu_A - \mu_P)^2 \sigma_B^2\)
A differs from the prior


\((\mu_B - \mu_P)^2 \sigma_A^2\)
B differs from the prior



Equation 14 — Simplified with flat prior (\(\sigma_P^2 \to \infty\)):
\[P(A, B \mid C = 1) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\mu_A - \mu_B)^2}{2(\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2)}\right) \tag{14}\]






NoteWhy does a flat prior simplify things?



When \(\sigma_P^2 \to \infty\), it dominates in both numerator and denominator. The first term \((\mu_A - \mu_B)^2 \sigma_P^2\) dominates the numerator; \(\sigma_P^2(\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2)\) dominates the denominator. They cancel, leaving only: how different are A and B from each other, relative to their combined noise?




Code
prob_common_cause <- function(d, sigma_A, sigma_B) {
  exp(-d^2 / (2 * (sigma_A^2 + sigma_B^2)))
}


Concrete example: If \(\sigma_T = 13.2°\), \(\sigma_F = 10°\), and \(d = 0\): P = \(\exp(0) = 1\). If \(d = 20°\): P = \(\exp(-400 / (2 \times 274.24)) = \exp(-0.73) = 0.48\). At \(d = 45°\): P = \(\exp(-2025/548.48) = \exp(-3.69) = 0.025\).

Visualization: The Causal Inference Gate


Code
d_ci <- seq(-90, 90, by = 1)
sigma_T_ci <- 13.2
sigma_F_ci <- 10.0

ci_gate <- tibble(
  d = d_ci,
  p_cc = prob_common_cause(d_ci, sigma_T_ci, sigma_F_ci)
)

ggplot(ci_gate, aes(x = d, y = p_cc)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3, color = "#E65100") +
  labs(
    title = "P(common cause | d) \u2014 The Causal Inference Gate (Eq. 14)",
    subtitle = bquote(sigma[T] == .(sigma_T_ci) * "," ~ sigma[F] == .(sigma_F_ci)),
    x = "Target-Flanker Difference (d)",
    y = "P(common cause)"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-90, 90, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.05, 1.15), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25))









When \(d = 0\) (identical items): \(P \approx 1\) → integrate fully. When \(d\) is large: \(P \approx 0\) → do not integrate.

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 15: CI Model Bias
In Cicchini et al.’s experiment, the two sources are the flanker compound (\(\sigma_C^2 = \sigma_F^2/2\)) and the target. Combining Eqs 12 and 14:
\[B = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_C^2 + \sigma_T^2} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{d^2}{2(\sigma_C^2 + \sigma_T^2)}\right) \cdot d \tag{15}\]


Code
ci_bias <- function(d, sigma_T, sigma_F) {
  sigma_C2 <- sigma_F^2 / 2
  w_max <- sigma_T^2 / (sigma_C2 + sigma_T^2)
  p_cc <- exp(-d^2 / (2 * (sigma_C2 + sigma_T^2)))
  w_max * p_cc * d
}

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
section: Equation 16: CI Bias with Free Parameters
text:
Equation 16: CI Bias with Free Parameters
For fitting real data, two free parameters (\(\beta\) for amplitude, \(\gamma\) for breadth) plus regression factor \(\rho = 0.67\):
\[B = \beta \rho \cdot \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_C^2 + \sigma_T^2} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{d^2}{2\gamma^2(\sigma_C^2 + \sigma_T^2)}\right) \cdot d \tag{16}\]


Code
ci_bias_full <- function(d, sigma_T, sigma_F, beta, rho, gamma) {
  sigma_C2 <- sigma_F^2 / 2
  w_ratio <- sigma_T^2 / (sigma_C2 + sigma_T^2)
  p_cc <- exp(-d^2 / (2 * gamma^2 * (sigma_C2 + sigma_T^2)))
  beta * rho * w_ratio * p_cc * d
}

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 17: Product of Two Gaussians
The product of two Gaussians with different means has a peak at:
\[\frac{1}{2\pi \sigma_A \sigma_B} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\mu_A - \mu_B)^2}{2(\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2)}\right) \tag{17}\]
This embeds the same Gaussian dependency on \(|\mu_A - \mu_B|\) as Eq 14 — the same gating behaviour emerges whether you compute the common-cause probability (Bayesian) or the distribution overlap (product).

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 18: Derivative-of-Gaussian Fit for Bias
Bias was fitted by a DoG — a Gaussian of width \(s\) multiplied by a straight line of slope \(a\):
\[B = a \cdot (\theta - m) \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\theta - m)^2}{s^2}\right) + b \tag{18}\]



Parameter
Meaning




\(a\)
Weight/amplitude (slope of linear component)


\(m\)
Centre of the DoG


\(s\)
Width of the Gaussian window


\(b\)
Vertical offset





Code
dog_fit <- function(theta, a, m, s, b) {
  a * (theta - m) * exp(-(theta - m)^2 / s^2) + b
}

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Equation 19: Gaussian Fit for Scatter
\[S = a \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\theta - m)^2}{s^2}\right) + b \tag{19}\]



Parameter
Meaning




\(a\)
Amplitude of the Gaussian dip (negative for U-shape)


\(m\)
Centre


\(s\)
Width (yoked to Eq 18)


\(b\)
Baseline scatter at large differences









NoteWhy yoke the width parameter?



Since bias and scatter likely originate from the same integration process, the width \(s\) is shared between Eq 18 and 19. This reduces free parameters and ensures both curves reflect the same integration window.




Code
gaussian_scatter_fit <- function(theta, a, m, s, b) {
  a * exp(-(theta - m)^2 / s^2) + b
}

title: Ideal Observer Model: Crowding Superiority
text:
Fitting Demonstration
We generate synthetic data from the IO model, add noise, and show how the DoG and Gaussian functions capture the underlying patterns.


Code
set.seed(42)
d_fit <- seq(-45, 45, by = 5)
sigma_T_fit <- 13.2
sigma_F_fit <- 10.0

w_fit <- optimal_weight(sigma_T_fit, sigma_F_fit, d_fit)
true_bias <- compute_bias(w_fit, d_fit)
true_scatter <- compute_scatter(w_fit, sigma_T_fit, sigma_F_fit)

observed_bias <- true_bias + rnorm(length(d_fit), 0, 0.5)
observed_scatter <- true_scatter + rnorm(length(d_fit), 0, 0.3)

df_obs <- data.frame(d = d_fit, bias = observed_bias, scatter = observed_scatter)

nls_bias <- nls(bias ~ a * (d - m) * exp(-(d - m)^2 / s^2) + b,
                data = df_obs, start = list(a = 0.3, m = 0, s = 20, b = 0))

nls_scatter <- nls(scatter ~ a * exp(-(d - m)^2 / s^2) + b,
                   data = df_obs, start = list(a = -4, m = 0, s = 20, b = 13))

theta_smooth <- seq(-45, 45, by = 0.5)
coef_b <- coef(nls_bias)
coef_s <- coef(nls_scatter)
fit_bias <- dog_fit(theta_smooth, coef_b["a"], coef_b["m"], coef_b["s"], coef_b["b"])
fit_scatter <- gaussian_scatter_fit(theta_smooth, coef_s["a"], coef_s["m"],
                                    coef_s["s"], coef_s["b"])

p_fit_bias <- ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(x = d_fit, y = observed_bias), size = 2.5, color = "#DC143C") +
  geom_line(aes(x = theta_smooth, y = fit_bias), linewidth = 1.2,
            color = "#DC143C", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Bias: DoG Fit (Eq. 18)",
       x = "Target-Flanker Difference (d)", y = "Bias (degrees)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-45, 45, 15))

p_fit_scatter <- ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sigma_T_fit, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(x = d_fit, y = observed_scatter), size = 2.5, color = "#2E8B57") +
  geom_line(aes(x = theta_smooth, y = fit_scatter), linewidth = 1.2,
            color = "#2E8B57", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Scatter: Gaussian Fit (Eq. 19)",
       x = "Target-Flanker Difference (d)", y = "Scatter (degrees)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-45, 45, 15))

p_fit_bias + p_fit_scatter +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Model Fitting Functions (Eq. 18\u201319)",
    subtitle = "Synthetic data from IO model + noise, fitted with DoG and Gaussian"
  )









The DoG captures the S-shaped bias pattern, while the inverted Gaussian captures the U-shaped scatter dip.

ImportantThe Three Predictions
